http://www.middleeaststar.com/news/27928.text: Who really benefits from the CIA chiefs Moscow trip RT.com 05 Sep 2026, 03:34 GMT+10 Ratcliffes hush-hush visit may be less about Moscow than helping turn Baltic alarm and Brussels money into new business for US arms makers Speculation abounds over the reason for CIA Director John Ratcliffe's recent trip to Moscow. Which probably could have been an email. Or a social media post. Just like everything else this administration does. Oooh, don't tell me! He went to demand that Russian President Vladimir Putin not help Iran! Or he went to ask whether they're still up for more speed dating to talk peace in Ukraine! Or maybe just to talk about swapping prisoners. Which happens fairly regularly. And doesn't require a personal visit. Or maybe Ratcliffe just had a jonesing for that ice cream at the GUM mall in Red Square. Who really knows. So I'd like to personally take the opportunity to add to the theories, which can only really be evaluated sometime down the road in hindsight. The thing that strikes me the most about this trip is the sudden secrecy. Specifically from an administration with a penchant for blabbing about everything. If Trump wanted to tell Putin or Russian intelligence something, he'd do it himself on Truth Social Instead, he was uncharacteristically vague, calling the trip semi-routine. When is this guy tight-lipped about anything? It's so far out of character for the American President that one is almost obligated to look for a motive for the secrecy. So with that in mind, it seems reasonable to ask whether there is any financial or political constituency that stands to benefit from the message being sent by this unusually secretive trip. Well, it turns out that it just happened to take place at the same time as the European Union was meeting to set its new 7-year budget, and Eastern European Baltic nations were making a massive push for cash from Brussels. You know what they say: if you have a pet that starts in with some nasty habits, like chewing the furniture to get your attention, then you really have to nip that in the bud real quick. Otherwise, there's a risk that, next thing you know, your other pets will learn from it and start gnawing on the couch or the table legs, too. So here you have Europe, that's been sitting there while Kiev says 'gimme money', and 'I deserve it because I'm defending all of Europe for you. Oh, and even better, actually, defending DEMOCRACY for you lazy bums'. And instead of whacking it on the nose and going, 'NO, BAD! Brussels just goes, 'Wanna treat?' So now, what do you know, here comes Latvia, who's been watching this whole charade, seeing that Ukraine goes from begging to getting tossed a bone every single time, and now they too are like, 'Woof, woof, I'm defending all of Europe for you. Where's my money? 7 BILLION EUROS, specifically'. And it's not like Latvia is even bothering to come up with its own twist on Ukraine's pitch. It's not like they're saying, 'Ukraine's pitch to Brussels is, 'Look, we're being invaded. You'd better give us what we want because we're the only thing standing between Putin showing up in Europe with a neck pillow for an Interrail tour of Europe.' So we, Latvia, need to come up with something else. Especially since we aren't actually being invaded - we just need some emotional-support money'. No, instead, they're just basically saying the exact same sort of thing minus the existential threat - that Latvia is the bouncer at the Baltic door keeping Putin on the other side of the velvet rope. Surely it can't possibly have anything to do with the fact that Latvia's economy could use the kind of economic boost that can only come from having Brussels dump a ton of cash into its defense industry, right? Because everything's going so well for Latvia economically, ever since this conflict in Ukraine went hot in 2022 and Riga cut itself off from Russian trade: from just over €2 billion a year back then, to just €193 million last year - an almost 90% reduction in the value of trade between the two countries, according to Latvia's own foreign affairs ministry. And now energy prices are going back up again, too - an 83% spike in gas prices since the beginning of this year in Latvia, and 24% over just the past month. An established trend since the EU cut everyone off from Russian fuel and now Trump's cutting everyone off from fuel from the Middle East with his apparently endless 'mine's bigger' standoff with Iran. Oh look, here comes Lithuania now, too. What a surprise! Another guy watching from the cheap seats and going: 'Hang on. We're also next to Russia. We have security problems, infrastructure costs, and defense bills. Where is OUR cash handout?' Turns out that Lithuania has just gone directly to Brussels with the invoice, essentially saying: You keep telling us the eastern flank is crucial to European security. Wonderful. Please prove this commitment using the traditional European unit of measurement: euros. When it comes to Eastern Europe, the EU's seven-year budget plan is starting to look like a group dinner where everyone suddenly remembers that the guy at the end of the table has a corporate credit card. But the real question is whose bills would Brussels ultimately be paying? Surely it's just a mere coincidence that major beneficiaries of Latvian and Lithuanian defense spending include Trump's America, as the largest supplier of major conventional arms to Latvia and Lithuania, according to the most recently available Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI)arms transfer data. All this comes after the western press reported that the CIA director flew to Moscow this week to tell Russia not to attack NATO countries. Which is actually great marketing for the cause of Eastern European countries shaking down Brussels and basically launching a grant program. They're behaving now as though a potential future hypothetical Russian attack on NATO is serious enough to justify enormous new expenditures, but the benefit of Brussels' largesse risks going to Washington as the top weapons supplier. The trip is remarkably convenient for governments seeking to turn fears about Russia into a case for vastly increased European defense spending - and for the American defense industry that stands to benefit from a big chunk of that spending. But hey, who really cares if everyone's barking out for treats when you're Brussels and all you ever need to do is reach into the pockets of the taxpayer. Even if you then run straight back to Uncle Sam with it and drop it in his lap. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8ly.text: Image source, Reuters/EPA Image caption, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky made an announcement concerning the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war last week - which South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has called "greatly disappointing" By Jake Kwon Seoul correspondent Published 28 September 2026 South Korea has summoned Ukraine's acting ambassador after President Volodymyr Zelensky last week announced his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo lodged a formal complaint with Andrii Vieshkin and expressed "strong regret" that Zelensky had revealed the transfer, which Seoul says was supposed to be a secret. The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. President Lee Jae Myung called the disclosure "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. Ukraine's foreign ministry declined to comment when approached by the BBC. In early 2025, Ukraine said its forces had captured two North Korean soldiers as prisoners of war in Russia's Kursk Oblast . After more than a year of negotiations between Seoul and Kyiv, Zelensky announced they had been transferred to South Korea at the UN General Assembly last Wednesday - adding they had not been "easy to capture alive". Seoul confirmed the news but sharply criticised Zelensky for allegedly breaking an agreement to keep the transfer a secret. This was partly to protect the North Koreans' families, President Lee's office said in a statement, which added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. Seoul demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. Lee faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure. The South Korean opposition accused him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. Lee, whose party takes a conciliatory approach to the North, has been making efforts to reopen peace talks, with little success. Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. "When North Korea actively participates in a war in Europe, South Korea cannot remain a distant observer," said Mykhailo Podolyak, a senior adviser to Zelensky. "The transfer of defence technologies and capabilities from Seoul to Kyiv is not just about helping Ukraine; it is about South Korea protecting its own long-term security interests by containing the expansion of an aggressive totalitarian axis." This July, Seoul announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: Pope Leo XIV has clashed with Milei, albeit indirectly, over AI, labour rights and disability. Photograph: Evandro Inetti/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Pope Leo XIV has clashed with Milei, albeit indirectly, over AI, labour rights and disability. Photograph: Evandro Inetti/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Pope Leo XIV Pope’s visit to Argentina sets up showdown with ‘hyper-capitalist’ Milei President has opposing views on many issues, and once called Leo’s predecessor the ‘representative of the Evil One’ Facundo Iglesia in Buenos Aires Sun 8 Nov 2026 04.00 EST Last modified on Sun 8 Nov 2026 04.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina. But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei , has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding. “[The government] cut off the supply of medications, special foods and diapers. They haven’t delivered any since last November. The matter is in court,” said the facility’s coordinator, Fernando Montero. The pope and Milei, he said, “have completely opposing ideologies”, arguing that the pope teaches that a person’s worth is not measured by whether they are productive, whereas Milei is a “hyper-capitalist” who believes only “those who compete the most should be rewarded”. Pope Leo’s three days here – he began a three-country trip through South America in Uruguay on Friday, and will finish with six days in Peru – will be the first papal visit to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987. His predecessor, Pope Francis, who was Argentine, never returned during his papacy. The trip could prove uncomfortable for Milei. A far-right libertarian economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as the symbol of his promised spending cuts, Milei called Francis an “imbecile” and “the representative of the Evil One on Earth” in 2020, and accused him of promoting communism, saying social justice was theft. Milei claims to have apologised when he met Francis in the Vatican in February 2024. Since taking office the previous December, he has slashed public spending, which the government says was needed to curb inflation. The cost, however, was high. The thinktank Mate estimates that retirees on the minimum pension – 63% of the total – have lost about 30% of their purchasing power. Last Wednesday at the weekly retirees’ march outside Congress, a man held up a cardboard sign reading, “Save us Pope Leo XIV – Milei is killing us.” Last month, Buenos Aires archbishop Jorge García Cuerva said Leo XIV would find “a divided Argentina and a large number of very poor brothers and sisters.” But the differences between the pope and the president go beyond typical social issues. In May, Leo XIV called for “disarming” artificial intelligence, while Milei has said he would not regulate AI technology and has instead presented bills to build datacentres across the country and to grant legal status to “no-human corporations”. Federico Sturzenegger, a minister in charge of state cuts, says he has used AI to draft legislation. Milagros Miceli, a sociologist and computer scientist who leads the Critical AI Lab in Berlin, said the “contradiction” between the two is “pretty evident”. She welcomed Leo’s visit, celebrating how the “powerful figure” of the pope intends to put “human beings at the centre by stripping these technologies of the values that are presented to us as taking precedence over humanity.” Juan Grabois, a left-wing Peronist deputy and social leader who served in the Vatican’s Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, said: “The idea of absolute deregulation is at the heart of the president’s agenda, and the replacement of the human element with these forms of algorithmic power has clearly also become a policy priority for the government.” Disability funding has been a flashpoint between church and state. As Milei has clashed with Congress over a funding law that remains in limbo, Argentina’s conference of bishops wrote to the health minister, Mario Lugones, on 1 April, denouncing “the serious situation facing numerous institutions dedicated to the care and support of people with disabilities in our country”. The ministry has met the bishops twice since, in April and again on 5 October, but without resolving the impasse. The government is trying to downplay potential tensions. “There’s no way the pope is going to come here to comment on local politics,” Sandra Pettovello, the minister overseeing social policy, said recently. Amnesty International, meanwhile, has written to the pope about Argentina, warning of its “concern about government decisions that affect the exercise of fundamental rights”. All of this will be top of mind when Milei receives the pope at the airport on Sunday. From the disability home, the pope will go on to Buenos Aires and meet business and union leaders; then on Tuesday he will celebrate Mass at the grounds of FAdeA, the state-owned military aircraft factory in Córdoba, whose workers have protested against Milei’s cuts. Juan Cruz Esquivel, director of Buenos Aires University’s Barometer of Religions and Beliefs, says the itinerary speaks for itself. “I don’t want to speculate [about what the pope will say], but clearly any mention of defending domestic production, labour, disability or social justice in the pope’s rhetoric naturally clashes with the ideology that Milei’s government has been promoting,” says Esquivel. Mariano Oberlin, a Catholic priest in an impoverished neighbourhood of Córdoba, expects the clash to play out diplomatically. “Pope Leo has been saying it without confronting, but he keeps upholding the church’s social doctrine as the key axis of his ministry,” Oberlin said. “If Milei wants to use him, he’ll probably have to do a lot of juggling to make him say the opposite of what he’s been saying – and of what he’ll surely say when he comes: that the Gospel invites us to feel like brothers, to respect each person’s deep, inherent dignity, and to fight so that this dignity becomes real in access to rights.” Since Francis’s tenure, social movements in Latin America have come closer to the Catholic church, and Argentina is no exception. Grabois, who was part of that process, sees the relationship as a two-way exchange. “[Francis] wasn’t the ‘good priest’ who came to help the poor,” he says, arguing that the exchanges helped Francis “develop his social thinking”. “Without the cartoneros (cardboard pickers) and the villeros (people from impoverished neighbourhoods), Francis would not have been Francis.” To Grabois, the same is true for Leo. “Francis took notice of Leo because he saw him supporting the Peruvian indigenous movement.” That doesn’t mean all Argentine social movements support the pope. On Saturday, a day before the visit, the LGBTQIA+ community will hold the 35th Pride March in Buenos Aires. María Rachid from the march’s organising committee said: “The church’s dogma regarding our families has not changed at any time, neither under the previous pope nor under this one”, though she notes that Francis’s words on gay rights “brought some relief to many families and their communities”. But a new development is the rise of evangelical churches, while Catholic identification falls. Buenos Aires University found 57.7% of Argentines identify as Catholic and 17.4% as evangelical, compared with 76.5% and 9% nearly 20 years ago. Last week, Milei inaugurated an evangelical temple in Neuquén and gave a nakedly political speech promising to seek re-election next year. Although Catholicism remains Argentina’s majority religion, it has lost its cultural hegemony and its influence on legislative agenda, Esquivel said.
